{{distinguish|Dushnik–Miller theorem}}
In the mathematical theory of [[infinite graph]]s, the '''Erdős–Dushnik–Miller theorem''' is a form of [[Ramsey's theorem]] stating that every infinite graph contains either a [[Countable set|countably infinite]] [[independent set (graph theory)|independent set]], or a [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] with the same [[cardinality]] as the whole graph.{{r|milpou}}

The theorem was first published by {{harvs|first1=Ben|last1=Dushnik|first2=E. W.|last2=Miller|year=1941|txt}}, in both the form stated above and an equivalent [[Complement graph|complementary form]]: every infinite graph contains either a countably infinite clique or an independent set with equal cardinality to the whole graph. In their paper, they credited [[Paul Erdős]] with assistance in its proof. They applied these results to the [[comparability graph]]s of [[partially ordered set]]s to show that each partial order contains either a countably infinite [[antichain]] or a [[Total order|chain]] of cardinality equal to the whole order, and that each partial order contains either a countably infinite chain or an antichain of cardinality equal to the whole order.{{r|dusmil}}

The same theorem can also be stated as a result in [[set theory]], using the [[infinitary combinatorics|arrow notation]] of {{harvtxt|Erdős|Rado|1956}}, as <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\kappa,\alef_0)^2</math>. This means that, for every set <math>S</math> of cardinality <math>\kappa</math>, and every partition of the ordered pairs of elements of <math>S</math> into two subsets <math>P_1</math> and <math>P_2</math>, there exists either a subset <math>S_1\subset S</math> of cardinality <math>\kappa</math> or a subset <math>S_2\subset S</math> of cardinality <math>\alef_0</math>, such that all pairs of elements of <math>S_i</math> belong to <math>P_i</math>.{{r|partcalc}} Here, <math>P_1</math> can be interpreted as the edges of a graph having <math>S</math> as its vertex set, in which <math>S_1</math> (if it exists) is a clique of cardinality <math>\kappa</math>, and <math>S_2</math> (if it exists) is a countably infinite independent set.{{r|milpou}}

If <math>S</math> is taken to be the [[cardinal number]] <math>\kappa</math> itself, the theorem can be formulated in terms of [[ordinal number]]s with the notation  <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\kappa,\omega)^2</math>, meaning that <math>S_2</math> (when it exists) has [[order type]] <math>\omega</math>. For uncountable [[regular cardinal]]s <math>\kappa</math> (and some other cardinals) this can be strengthened to <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\kappa,\omega+1)^2</math>;{{r|singular}} however, it is [[Consistency|consistent]] that this strengthening does not hold for the [[cardinality of the continuum]].{{r|ss}}

The Erdős–Dushnik–Miller theorem has been called the first "unbalanced" generalization of Ramsey's theorem, and Paul Erdős's first significant result in set theory.{{r|hajnal}}
